newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-German government faces pension battle.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-German government faces pension battle.

text.p: The German government on Monday faced the unwelcome prospect of having to push a major pension reform through parliament after opposition Social Democrats (SPD) refused to enter special talks over reform proposals.

Bonn's main opposition SPD said they would not take up government offers to discuss a planned reform of the country's pension system that they believe will leave millions of pensioners on the breadline.

While an overhaul of the pension system does not need the SPD's agreement, the lack of cross-party support means the reform could turn into a potentially damaging 1998 campaign issue for Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU).
"The Social Democrats will not have any part in pension cuts that will leave millions of pensions requiring welfare support," the SPD said in a statement after a meeting of party executives in Bonn.

Kohl's government wants to reduce pension levels to cope with the ageing German population and as part of structural reforms it says are necessary with increasingly globalised economies and ahead of Europe's planned monetary union.
Current proposals envisage dropping pension levels to 64 percent of average net wages from around 70 percent.
Earlier, Kohl called on the SPD to back the reform that the government is seeking to pass into law by the end of the year.
Speaking before a meeting of his CDU, Kohl said both parties should be prepared to make compromises on the reform.
"There is no way however that the legislation on both pension and (a separate) tax reform will not bear our imprint," Kohl told German television.
SPD chief Oskar Lafontaine said his party was ready to debate the reform within normal parliamentary business and that any decisions should have the backing of wide parliamentary majority.

The SPD also demanded that the government specify how a proposed transfer of around 15 billion marks ($9 billion) in non-welfare costs from the state pension fund to the federal budget would be achieved.
German Labour Minster Norbert Bluem attacked the SPD's decision not to seek a package that would have cross-party support as a "flight from joint responsibility".

"This is new in the post-war history of pension reform. By distancing themselves from the process, they are the ones who are stoking the fears of the pensioners," he said in a statement. ($ = 1.668 German Marks)
